title: Bishops: squares, pairs and trades
outcomes: Counts a bishop's squares to judge how active it is
Sees how a shut-in bishop leaves its pawns undefended
Decides when giving up a bishop wins something concrete

steps.text:
A bishop is worth what its diagonals allow. Count the squares it can reach and ask what it attacks. A bishop shut in behind its own pawns has little to do.
**Rule of thumb:** pawns on the colour of your own bishop make it harder to use. Two bishops together cover both colours, which helps most when the position is open.

steps.caption: Black to move. Look at the bishop on c8.

claims.statement: The bishop on c8 has no legal move.

steps.text:
A bishop that cannot move cannot defend anything. In the next position White can use that.
Ask of each bishop: **how many squares does it have, and does it guard what needs guarding?** Count the squares before you decide which minor piece to keep.

steps.title: Same pawns, a different bishop
steps.prompt: Black's bishop is the dark-squared one on f8. Does Ng5 still win material? Predict first, then check.

steps.text: Two bishops are not always worth keeping. When trading one for a knight wins something concrete, such as a pawn that knight alone defended, take the gain. Before you give up a bishop, count: **who defends the pawn, and what is left after the trade?**

steps.title: Same trade, one defender more
steps.prompt: Black has an extra pawn on d6 that also defends e5. Does Bxc6 still win a pawn? Predict first, then check.
